resources.string: One oligodendrocyte can extend processes to several segments in the central nervous system.
This wrapping insulates an axon segment. The gaps are nodes, not breaks in the axon.
Microglial processes survey the surrounding tissue.
Microglia are resident immune cells of the central nervous system and can clear debris.
Motile cilia help move cerebrospinal fluid locally along the ventricular surface.
This layer lines the ventricle. It is not the specialized choroid plexus epithelium.
Flattened satellite glia surround neuronal cell bodies in peripheral ganglia.
The central neuron provides context. These glia are distinct from Schwann cells on axons.
Absorbed photons can initiate phototransduction in the outer segment. Rods are especially important in dim light.
Light changes glutamate release here. The optic nerve spike train is generated downstream.
Different cone types respond to different wavelength ranges. Comparing their activity supports color vision.
The broader terminal relays graded changes in transmitter release.
These projections are adjacent to photoreceptor outer segments. RPE supports the visual cycle and clears shed material.
Melanin-containing granules help reduce stray light.
The dendrites receive processed signals in the inner retina.
Ganglion cell axons carry spikes out of the retina and form the optic nerve.
Deflection changes mechanosensitive channel activity. This view illustrates a cochlear inner hair cell.
The hair cell releases transmitter onto a nerve ending. The sensory nerve carries the spike signal.
Odorants contact receptor-bearing cilia that extend from the dendritic knob.
The axon exits the epithelium toward the olfactory bulb.
Apical microvilli contact molecules dissolved in saliva.
Taste cells signal to sensory fibers. The signaling mechanism depends on the cell subtype.
Superficial cells help maintain the tear-facing barrier.
Basal cells lie near the basement membrane, below the flatter superficial cells.
Merkel cell in the basal epidermis
This cell is part of a touch receptor complex in the basal epidermis.
A sensory neurite contacts the Merkel cell. The complex contributes to sustained touch and texture perception.
Bipolar cells receive photoreceptor input. Rod and cone bipolar cell types participate in different circuits.
The terminal passes a graded signal. AII amacrine cells are a key relay for rod bipolar output.
AII amacrine cells receive rod bipolar input in the primary dim-light circuit.
Electrical connections carry signals to ON cone bipolar cells. Other AII connections are not shown.
Outer segments lie beside the supporting pigment epithelium. Incoming light passes through the inner retina first.
Bipolar and amacrine circuits relay and shape signals before ganglion cells send them out.
The gold arrow points toward the outer segments, from the inner side of the retina.
The blue arrow points back toward the ganglion layer. This is separate from the direction that light travels.
Rod photoreceptors respond to dim light
Rod bipolar cells relay through AII amacrine cells
Cones use cone bipolar cells under brighter conditions
Ganglion cell axons carry the signal into the optic nerve
Rod bipolar → AII → ON cone bipolar
Two representative ON routes are shown. This is not a complete wiring map. Photoreceptor signals are graded, while ganglion cells send spikes.
Chance of at least one absorption
Poisson model: probability of at least one absorption = 1 − exp(−λ).
The window is fixed and events are modeled as independent. This is the probability of an absorption event, not the probability of seeing or a personal vision threshold.
rod bipolar cone bipolar retinal relay
Relays graded signals between photoreceptors and the inner retinal circuit.
ON and OFF pathways respond differently
The bipolar cell passes a graded signal to its terminal
Rod bipolar output can reach AII amacrine cells
Passes rod bipolar signals into downstream retinal pathways.
AII cells relay that signal in the inner retina
Electrical connections carry the signal to ON cone bipolars
Cone bipolar output can drive ganglion cell signaling
